title: The tree — cut it, it bleeds; leave it, it lives (6.11)
hook: strike a great tree at the root and sap runs out, but it lives; when life leaves a branch, the branch dries up

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rivers and the sea, from sea to sea, not knowing I am this river. Your line was the sea. Did a glass of water remind you? Day three hundred forty-seven.
screen: `THE RIVERS AND THE SEA — THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Find an old tree with a scar on it: a place where a branch was cut, or a car hit it, or someone carved initials years ago. Often you'll see where the sap ran, dried now into a hard, shiny crust. The tree bled. And it's still standing, still leafing out every spring. Next to it, maybe, there's one branch that's gray and bare, that never came back. Same tree. One part alive, one part not. Uddalaka takes his son out to a tree like that.
screen: `AN OLD TREE WITH A SCAR.` → `IT BLED, AND IT'S STILL STANDING.` → `ONE GRAY BRANCH.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: my dear, if someone were to strike this great tree at its root, it would bleed sap, but it would live. Strike it in the middle, it would bleed, but live. Strike it at the top, it would bleed, but live. Filled through and through by the living self, it stands, drinking in water, rejoicing. Then: if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If it leaves a second, that one dries up. If it leaves a third, that dries up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. And then the line that turns it toward his son. In the same way, my dear, understand this: the body dies when life leaves it. But life does not die. Notice the order of the lesson. First, life is everywhere in the tree: root, middle, top. You can wound it in any of those places and it carries on, because life isn't sitting in one spot that you could cut out. It pervades. Second, the body depends on life, not the other way around. A dry branch isn't the death of life. It's life leaving that branch. For Uddalaka, the same is true of us. The body is a tree. Something fills it, makes it drink and grow and rejoice, and when that something leaves, the body falls. But what left doesn't fall with it. Hindus have drawn on lines like this at the bedside of the dying and at funerals for many centuries. And once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this. You are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `STRIKE IT: IT BLEEDS, BUT LIVES.` · `DRINKING IN WATER, REJOICING.` · `LIFE LEAVES A BRANCH; IT DRIES.` · `THE BODY DIES. LIFE DOES NOT.` · then, large: `LIFE PERVADES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice feels the life in the tree. Sit and settle. Bring your attention to your feet, your roots. Feel that something is alive there: warmth, tingling, pulse. Move up to your middle: belly, chest, the breath moving. Then to your top: face, scalp. The same life, root to crown. Rest in it, the way the tree stands drinking in water, rejoicing. The bell holds the time.
The tree. Uddalaka's great tree, filled by the living self: wounded, it lives; when life leaves, it dries; the body dies, but life does not.
Your line: life pervades. Today, stop by one tree or plant for a moment, and notice that it is drinking, growing, alive in every part. Day three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: At Hindu deathbeds and funerals, families often recite or reflect on scriptures that teach that the self does not die with the body, from the Upanishads to the Bhagavad Gita's second chapter.

fork.setup: you strike a great tree at its root, then in the middle, then at the top. what happens?
options: it dies at the first blow.
it bleeds sap each time, but lives.
fork.reveal: it bleeds, but lives, because life fills the whole tree. only when life leaves does a branch, or the whole tree, dry up.

original.note: Sanskrit jīva: living, a living being. the tree is filled by the jīva ātman, the living self.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lesson about trees.
what it means: life fills the whole body; the body depends on it; when it leaves, the body dies, but life does not.

what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.11.1–3, jivena atmana anuprabhutah, filled by the living self; the line 'this dies when life leaves it, life does not die' is a key early statement on the self's survival.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.11.1–3 (the tree; the body dies, life does not; the refrain)
Bhagavad Gita 2 (the self does not die)

notes: 'Bleed' renders the text's word for oozing sap (sravet); confirm.
The text names a first, second and third branch; kept.
Claim that Hindus have drawn on such lines at deathbeds and funerals 'for many centuries' is general; confirm or soften.
